hints: Look at the textures in Fig. 1.1. Find the large pale oval shapes with no membranes inside, and separately find the grainy grey background fluid that fills the whole chloroplast.
Recall where excess triose phosphate is converted to insoluble storage carbohydrate, and where the soluble enzymes for carbon fixation are located.
walkthrough:
Spot the storage product**
Photosynthesis makes triose phosphate, and any excess is joined together to make starch for temporary storage in the chloroplast. In a TEM starch shows up as large, pale, rounded bodies because it is not membrane-bound and stains lightly. Those are the white ovals at the bottom right and middle of Fig. 1.1.

Spot the fluid for the Calvin cycle**
The light independent stage needs soluble enzymes like rubisco dissolved in water. That watery matrix is the stroma, the grey granular background that surrounds all the thylakoid membranes. So A points to a starch grain and B points to the stroma background.
Final answer: A - starch grain (large electron-lucent oval structure, bottom right). B - stroma (aqueous matrix filling chloroplast around thylakoids).

hints: Structure C is the dark stacked disc region where many membranes are piled tightly on top of each other.
walkthrough:
Name the stack**
The dark bands in the micrograph are stacks of thylakoid membranes. A single stack is called a granum. That is what label C is pointing to.
Final answer: C is a granum (plural grana).

hints: Start from what C is made of - think about how many separate flattened sacs are piled together there.
Think about what must be housed in those membranes for catching light, and why having many folded layers helps.
Link the membrane proteins to what happens in the light dependent stage - electron flow and ATP making.
Build a clear chain: membrane structure -> more pigment and protein -> more light absorption and photophosphorylation.
walkthrough:
Stacks mean more membrane**
A granum is a stack of thylakoid discs. Stacking packs a huge area of thylakoid membrane into a tiny volume of chloroplast. In biology, more membrane means more room for membrane proteins.

More membrane means more light capture**
Embedded in that membrane are chlorophyll and other pigments arranged in photosystems and light-harvesting complexes. A larger area holds many more pigment molecules, so much more light energy can be absorbed per chloroplast.

More membrane means more chemistry**
The same membrane also holds the electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase stalked particles. That allows many electron flows and much chemiosmotic ATP production at once.

Tie to function**
All of this serves the light dependent stage. Light absorption, water splitting, NADP reduction and photophosphorylation all happen on or across the thylakoid membrane, so the granum structure maximises the rate of that stage.

Final answer: C is a stack of thylakoids forming large membrane surface area for photosynthetic pigments / photosystems for absorption of light energy and for many electron carriers / ETC proteins / ATP synthase for the light dependent stage / photophosphorylation.

hints: Remember rubisco can accept two different gases at the same active site, and high temperature makes stomata close so one gas builds up inside the leaf.
Think about what happens to RuBP and carbon fixation if the wrong gas wins, and what that wasteful process is called.
walkthrough:
Rubisco has two jobs**
Rubisco normally carboxylates RuBP by adding carbon dioxide. But oxygen fits the same active site, so rubisco also acts as an oxygenase. It is really a competition between $CO_2$ and $O_2$ for RuBP.

Heat favours oxygen**
At high temperatures C3 plants close stomata to save water, so $CO_2$ cannot enter and $O_2$ from photosynthesis builds up. Oxygen then combines with RuBP instead of carbon dioxide. This starts photorespiration, which releases $CO_2$ and uses ATP without making sugar, so net carbon fixation and photosynthesis fall.
Final answer: At high temperature oxygen reacts with RuBP catalysed by rubisco instead of carbon dioxide, causing photorespiration; less / no carbon fixation so rate of photosynthesis falls.

hints: Read Fig. 1.2 at 30 million years ago - describe what is happening to atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration around that time.
If carbon dioxide falls while oxygen from C3 photosynthesis stays high, think about what happens to the O2 to CO2 ratio and to rubisco.
Think about why a new carbon-concentrating system would give higher fitness and spread by natural selection just when photorespiration becomes severe.
walkthrough:
Read the fall in CO2**
In Fig. 1.2, from 50 to about 35 million years ago $CO_2$ stays high near 850 to 1000 parts per million. Then around 30 million years ago it drops steeply from about 900 toward 500 parts per million and keeps falling to about 250 parts per million by 20 million years ago.

Link to rubisco competition**
C3 photosynthesis itself was adding oxygen to the air while $CO_2$ was falling, so the oxygen to carbon dioxide ratio became high. That makes rubisco favour the oxygenase reaction, so C3 plants suffer severe photorespiration and low growth.

Explain the origin of C4**
Any variant able to pump $CO_2$ around rubisco and avoid photorespiration would photosynthesise faster and leave more offspring. Oxygen therefore acted as a selection pressure, giving C4 plants a selective advantage that explains why they first appeared 30 million years ago when $CO_2$ fell.

Final answer: Fig. 1.2 shows atmospheric $CO_2$ falling sharply around 30 million years ago from about 900 to below 600 parts per million; O2 to $CO_2$ ratio rises so rubisco increasingly reacts with oxygen causing photorespiration in C3 plants; C4 anatomy gives selective advantage in these conditions so C4 plants evolved and spread.
